MEASURED CONCLUSION, and it contradicts the property this test was written to confirm.
The hypothesis was: read volume scales with the POSITION of to_ts and never with the
WIDTH of the window. Measured, read_rows is IDENTICAL across all three windows at the
full delta table. It scales with NEITHER position nor width. The hypothesis is false
for rows and true only for read_bytes, which does track the position of to_ts.
Why: `minute` is the LAST column of the ORDER BY, deliberately, so that a time predicate
cannot prune the prefix a cumulative sum needs. That choice is what makes the curve
correct for a window opening mid-stream, and its unavoidable price is that no time
predicate prunes GRANULES either. The `minute < to_ts` push-down reduces bytes
decompressed, not rows scanned.
The honest statement of this design is therefore: READ VOLUME SCALES WITH THE SIZE OF
THE CORPUS, and only a DIMENSION filter reduces it (platform prunes to 16,384 rows of
30,662, evidence: filter_shapes). That is a real scaling limit, not a pass, and it is
exactly what makes the 100x question a day-boundary-snapshot question.
What the old test got right by accident: reads really are equal for end_1h and
whole_corpus. What it got wrong was concluding anything from that, because it compared
two windows sharing an upper bound and never varied the thing it claimed to test.
